implementation_statement: Access control policy POL-02 was adopted in 2023 and re-approved 2026-09-17, effective 2026-10-01 (P06). Procedures for quarterly access reviews, privileged access, and non-employee account end dates are being written under STD-06.

provider_if_inherited: Identity provider vendor (SOC 2 Type 2); EHR vendor (SOC 2 Type 2)
implementation_statement: Employee accounts are provisioned in the identity provider from the HR system feed and federated to the EHR, PACS, and cloud accounts; terminations disable access automatically. Contracted clinicians, agency nurses, and affiliated practice users are created by ticket with no end date and depend on the agencies and practices to report departures (gap 8): 19 active accounts of departed users were found in July 2026. Access reviews are annual (last February 2026), not quarterly. The EHR role catalog has 64 roles.
evidence: HR feed configuration; IdP and EHR exports; access review record February 2026; July 2026 stale-account report

implementation_statement: Employee lifecycle is automated through the HR-driven identity provider workflow. Non-employee accounts (contracted, agency, affiliated practice) are created manually and are not covered by automation.
evidence: IdP provisioning logs; non-employee account tickets

implementation_statement: The identity provider disables accounts after 45 days of inactivity. Local accounts on the on-premises clinical servers (LIS, cardiology, fetal surveillance) and on medical device workstations are not covered.
evidence: IdP inactivity policy; directory stale-account report

provider_if_inherited: Identity provider vendor (SOC 2 Type 2); MSSP (SOC 2 Type 2)
implementation_statement: Account creation, changes, and privilege grants in the identity provider, directory, and cloud are logged and sent to the SIEM, with alerts for new domain administrators. EHR security-role changes are logged in the EHR audit trail but are not alerted.
evidence: SIEM use case list; directory audit policy

implementation_statement: The EHR enforces role-based access from its 64-role catalog; break-the-glass access to restricted records (VIP, employee, behavioral health) requires a reason and is logged. File shares and the data warehouse use directory groups.
evidence: EHR security class report; break-the-glass configuration

implementation_statement: Firewalls control traffic between the campus, the outpatient center, the cloud hub, and the internet. Infusion pumps and imaging modalities sit on their own VLANs with deny-by-default rules. Patient monitors, fetal monitors, the catheterization lab system, laboratory analyzers, and dispensing cabinets share the clinical workstation VLAN (gap 1), and building OT shares the IT network at the main campus (gap 13).
evidence: Firewall rule export; VLAN map; network diagram (P04)

implementation_statement: Duties are separated between IT (administration), the Information Security Manager (monitoring and review), and HR (identity source). Gaps: the 2 backup administrators also hold domain administrator rights, and the PACS vendor administers both the application and its server operating systems.

EHR roles follow least privilege. Outside the EHR, 31 accounts hold domain administrator rights, including 12 vendor service accounts (gap 4). Pharmacy, laboratory, and imaging super-user roles in the EHR have not been reviewed since 2024.
evidence: Directory privileged group export; EHR super-user list

implementation_statement: IT administrators have separate administrator accounts for the directory and cloud. Two IT staff use one account for both daily work and server administration, and vendor service accounts are used interactively by vendor engineers.

Privileged access management with just-in-time elevation covers the 5 cloud accounts only. Directory, identity provider, EHR administration, PACS, LIS, and network device administration use standing privileges (gap 4). Extension funded for 2027 Q1.
evidence: Privileged access broker configuration; FY2027 budget approval
regulatory_driver: C-HPH-R08 (CPG Essential: Separate User and Privileged Accounts)

implementation_statement: The identity provider locks accounts after 10 failed attempts for 15 minutes and applies risk-based sign-in blocking; the EHR applies the same lockout to its native sign-in.
evidence: IdP lockout policy; EHR security settings

implementation_statement: A system use notification is shown at directory, VPN, and EHR sign-in, and on administrator consoles, stating that access is monitored and limited to authorized use.

Shared clinical workstations lock after 10 minutes and badge-tap single sign-on lets the next user switch quickly; offices lock after 15 minutes. ED tracking board and nursing station display workstations are exempt and stay signed in to a generic account.
The EHR ends sessions after 30 minutes of inactivity on workstations and 15 minutes on remote sessions; the portal times out after 20 minutes.

Employee remote access uses the identity provider with MFA and device checks. Of 46 vendors with remote access, 32 use the vendor access platform with MFA, recording, and approval; 14 device and application vendors use persistent VPN accounts without MFA (gap 5).
evidence: Remote access inventory; VPN account list; vendor access platform logs

implementation_statement: VPN and vendor access platform sessions are logged to the SIEM. Persistent vendor VPN tunnels are not monitored for session activity.

Clinical Wi-Fi uses enterprise authentication with certificates for managed devices; infusion pumps use a dedicated wireless network with its own credentials; guest Wi-Fi is isolated from internal networks.

380 clinical smartphones and all laptops are enrolled in mobile device management with encryption, passcodes, and remote wipe. Contracted physicians use personal phones for secure messaging through an app container; 60 personal devices have not enrolled the container.
evidence: MDM inventory; secure messaging enrollment report

implementation_statement: Affiliated practice users and contracted physicians reach the EHR from devices the hospital does not manage. The affiliated practice services agreement sets minimum device requirements (supported OS, screen lock, anti-malware), but compliance is not checked.
evidence: Affiliated practice services agreement; conditional access policy

implementation_statement: Security awareness requirements are in POL-01 and POL-05. A training standard covering contracted clinicians and affiliated practice users is not yet written.

Employees complete annual security and privacy training (96% in 2025) and receive quarterly phishing simulations (June 2026 click rate 6.9%). Contracted clinicians complete it through the Medical Staff Office (82%); affiliated practice users and agency nurses sign the acceptable use agreement but receive no training.
evidence: Training completion report; phishing simulation results
regulatory_driver: C-HPH-R01 (164.308(a)(5); 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(A); 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(B)); C-HPH-R08 (CPG Essential: Basic Cybersecurity Training)

implementation_statement: IT administrators receive vendor and cloud training. Clinical engineering staff and facilities engineers who administer networked devices and OT have no role-based security training.
Logging requirements appear in POL-03; the logging and monitoring standard (STD-02) is in draft (gap 10).

The SIEM receives EHR audit, identity provider, directory, firewall, VPN, EDR, email security, and cloud control-plane logs. Medical devices, OT, the LIS, the dispensing cabinet and pump servers, the cardiology system, the fetal surveillance server, and the interface engine do not send logs (gap 7).
evidence: SIEM source list; MSSP onboarding records

implementation_statement: EHR and identity provider audit records include user, patient, action, time, workstation, and outcome; cloud and firewall logs include source, destination, and action.

control_name: Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting
implementation_statement: The MSSP reviews and escalates security alerts 24x7. EHR access review covers only VIP records and employees viewing their own or coworkers' records; there is no broad inappropriate-access analytics (gap 7). About 30 VIP alerts a month are reviewed by the Privacy Officer.
evidence: MSSP monthly report; EHR VIP access reports
regulatory_driver: C-HPH-R01 (164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D); 164.308(a)(5)(ii)(C)); C-HPH-R08 (CPG Enhanced: Centralized Log Collection)

implementation_statement: SIEM correlation rules run for identity, endpoint, and cloud events. EHR audit data reaches the SIEM but has no correlation use cases beyond VIP alerts.
Logs are forwarded to the SIEM and to a write-once log archive bucket in the security and log archive account; administrators of other accounts cannot delete them.
The SIEM keeps 1 year searchable; the log archive keeps 6 years for EHR audit and security logs. On-premises clinical servers keep local logs for 30 days or less.

Audit generation is enabled in the EHR, identity provider, directory, cloud, and firewalls. It is not enabled or not collected on the LIS, cardiology system, fetal surveillance server, and device management consoles.
The co-sourced internal audit firm assesses controls each year; the 2026 assessment (P07) covered 34 controls from 2026-07-27 to 2026-08-14.

Interfaces with the clearinghouse, HIE, reference laboratory, teleradiology group, and public health agencies are documented in interface specifications and covered by BAAs or participation agreements. 6 legacy site-to-site VPNs (3 device vendors, 2 physician groups, 1 former reference laboratory) have no written interconnection terms; the former laboratory tunnel is still up.

The POA&M from P07 is tracked by the Information Security Manager and reported to the audit committee each quarter. Items from the 2025 risk analysis were tracked in a spreadsheet; 7 of 18 were still open at the 2026 analysis.

There is no federal authorization. The internal equivalent: the COO (system owner) accepted operation of HECS with conditions on 2026-09-17, and the CEO accepted the High risks with treatment plans (SSP section 4.2).

Continuous monitoring covers endpoints, identity, cloud posture, and quarterly vulnerability scans. Medical devices, OT, and on-premises clinical servers are outside monitoring until the SIEM onboarding project completes (2027-03-31).

Internal connections between the clinical VLAN, device VLANs, and the data center are documented for pumps and imaging only. Connections from monitors, analyzers, cabinets, and the catheterization lab to their servers are not documented.
Configuration management requirements are in POL-01; the configuration standard (STD-01) is in draft (gap 10).

Workstation and server images follow a benchmark-based baseline; cloud guardrails block public storage and unencrypted volumes. No documented baselines exist for network devices, the virtualization cluster, or vendor-managed clinical servers.

A weekly change advisory board approves infrastructure changes. EHR build changes go through the EHR change process with clinical sign-off. Changes made by device vendors through remote access are not recorded in change tickets.
evidence: Change tickets; EHR build change log

implementation_statement: Security impact is assessed for infrastructure changes on the change ticket. EHR upgrades that switch on new vendor features (for example the sepsis model in November 2025) had no security, privacy, or clinical safety impact review (gap 9).
evidence: Change ticket template; EHR upgrade notes

implementation_statement: Configuration settings are enforced by group policy and MDM for endpoints and by guardrails in the cloud. A benchmark scan of 10 servers in P07 found 23% of settings out of baseline; vendor-managed servers are not scanned.

Unneeded services are disabled on gold images. Medical device workstations and vendor-managed servers run vendor-defined services that have not been reviewed; SMBv1 remains enabled on 2 laboratory analyzer workstations.

IT assets are inventoried in the configuration management database. Biomedical engineering keeps a maintenance inventory of all medical devices, but the security inventory (network address, OS, support status, PHI storage) covers about 1,150 of 1,650 networked devices (70%), and MDS2 forms are on file for 35% of models (gap 1).
evidence: CMDB export; clinical engineering inventory; MDS2 register

implementation_statement: Inventory updates happen when IT or biomedical engineering installs a device. Passive network discovery to catch devices installed by vendors is funded for 2026 Q4.
Software is licensed through IT purchasing; the EHR license covers the 18 affiliated practices under the vendor's sublicensing terms.
Users cannot install software on managed endpoints; installation requires an IT ticket.
Contingency planning requirements are in POL-03; the contingency and recovery standard (STD-07) and an IT disaster recovery plan do not yet exist (gap 3).

Unit downtime procedures exist (2022) and the emergency operations plan covers short IT outages. There is no IT disaster recovery plan, and the emergency plan has no cyber hazard, no IT-outage diversion criteria, and no procedure for an outage longer than 4 hours (gaps 2 and 3). The BIA (P05) now supplies recovery objectives.
evidence: Unit downtime procedures; emergency operations plan; BIA

implementation_statement: Hurricane and mass-casualty plans are coordinated with the county emergency management agency and the regional healthcare coalition. IT recovery and the EHR vendor's disaster recovery are not coordinated with the emergency plan.

Essential functions (ED screening, inpatient care, births, emergency surgery) continue on paper during an outage; the order and timing of resuming each function are now set in the BIA but not yet written into procedures.
Critical assets for each essential function are identified in the BIA (P05 section 6) and in the HIPAA applications and data criticality analysis.
Emergency preparedness training is given at hire and every 2 years. Downtime training covers the 2022 unit procedures only; most staff hired since 2023 have not practiced paper workflows.

The EHR vendor tests its disaster recovery each year. The hospital has never restore-tested the LIS, dispensing cabinet server, pump server, monitoring gateway, fetal surveillance server, cardiology system, PACS, interface engine, or data warehouse. Downtime drills have never run beyond 4 hours (gap 3).
evidence: EHR vendor DR test summary; drill records

implementation_statement: Backups are stored in a separate backup account in a second region of the cloud provider, with separate credentials.

provider_if_inherited: EHR vendor (SOC 2 Type 2); Cloud provider (SOC 2 Type 2)
implementation_statement: The EHR vendor operates an alternate hosting site. Cloud workloads can be rebuilt in a second region from backups. There is no alternate processing site for the on-premises data center; recovery depends on rebuilding the virtualization cluster on site.
evidence: EHR vendor SOC 2 description; data center design

implementation_statement: The main campus has two internet carriers and the outpatient center two SD-WAN links. VoIP and smartphones depend on the campus network; analog lines and the EMS radio exist only in the ED and house supervisor office.

Cloud workloads are backed up daily and on-premises servers nightly to the backup appliance, which replicates to the backup account with 35-day write-once retention. Gaps: the backup appliance is joined to the hospital directory, and the fetal surveillance server and cardiology system are backed up by their vendors to local disks outside the appliance.
evidence: Backup job reports; backup account retention policy

implementation_statement: Backup jobs are checked daily for success. Restore testing is limited to single files from the file server (2 tests in 2026); no application-level restore has been tested.
evidence: Backup job reports; restore test records

implementation_statement: Recovery depends on rebuilding servers from backups; no documented recovery procedures exist for clinical servers, and no recovery time has been demonstrated against the BIA RTOs.
Identification and authentication requirements are in POL-02; the authenticator standard (STD-06) dates from 2023 and needs updating for phishing-resistant MFA and service accounts.

provider_if_inherited: Identity provider vendor (SOC 2 Type 2); EHR vendor (SOC 2 Type 2)
implementation_statement: Every employee, contracted clinician, and affiliated practice user has a unique account. Exceptions: generic accounts on ED tracking boards and nursing station displays, and shared local accounts on laboratory analyzer and catheterization lab workstations.
evidence: IdP and EHR user exports; generic account list

implementation_statement: MFA is enforced for privileged access to the cloud, identity provider, and EHR administration. Domain administrator sign-in on the campus network and vendor VPN accounts do not require MFA.

MFA is enforced for email, remote access, VPN, cloud, and EHR access from outside the hospital network. On campus, clinical workstations use badge tap plus password. 14 vendor VPN accounts lack MFA (gap 5).
evidence: Conditional access policy; badge single sign-on configuration

implementation_statement: The identity provider uses replay-resistant protocols and push MFA with number matching.
Managed endpoints and smartphones authenticate to Wi-Fi with certificates. Medical devices on the clinical VLAN connect without device authentication.
evidence: Wireless and network access control configuration

implementation_statement: Identifiers come from HR for employees. Non-employee identifiers are created by ticket and are not reused; affiliated practice user identifiers are requested by the practice manager with no verification of employment.
Passwords are 14 characters minimum with a banned list. Service account and vendor passwords are not vaulted or rotated; some vendor-managed servers and devices keep shared vendor passwords.
evidence: IdP password policy; service account list

implementation_statement: Patients authenticate to the EHR vendor's portal with identity proofing and optional MFA; external clinicians use the HIE's federated identity.
Incident response policy POL-03 was re-approved 2026-09-17 with two runbooks (P08). Procedures before then were a 2023 general plan.
IT and security staff are trained on incident roles. Clinical leaders, house supervisors, and the administrator-on-call rotation have no training on cyber incidents or the new runbooks.

A 2025 IT-only tabletop tested phishing; no exercise has tested ransomware with EHR downtime or diversion. A ransomware and 72-hour downtime tabletop is scheduled 2026-11-10 as the 482.15 additional exercise.

The MSSP triages and contains endpoint threats 24x7 and calls the Information Security Manager within 30 minutes on high severity. Incident handling for medical devices and OT has no defined steps, and the MSSP has no visibility of them.
All security and privacy incidents are logged in one incident register with discovery time and decision log since 2026-09 (P08).

Staff report incidents through the service desk or the privacy hotline. Notification duties are mapped in the P08 matrix; the decision log for breach determinations was missing for 3 of 9 privacy incidents sampled from 2025-2026.
The MSSP provides incident response support; the cyber insurer's panel provides counsel and forensics.
The incident response plan and the two P08 runbooks were approved 2026-09-17; they are not yet tested or integrated into the emergency operations plan.
Biomedical engineering schedules and records maintenance for all medical devices. IT maintenance is ticketed. Device maintenance performed remotely by manufacturers is not recorded locally.
32 vendors use the vendor access platform with approval, MFA, and session recording. 14 vendors keep persistent VPN accounts without MFA or recording (gap 5).
evidence: Vendor access platform logs; VPN account list

implementation_statement: On-site vendor engineers sign in at biomedical engineering and are escorted in clinical areas; remote vendor engineers on persistent VPN accounts are not individually identified.
Media protection requirements are in POL-04; procedures for medical device drives returned to manufacturers are missing.

IT media is destroyed by a certified vendor with certificates. Hard drives in imaging modalities, ultrasound units, and leased copiers are returned to vendors without a sanitization certificate in 4 of 6 returns reviewed.
Physical security requirements are in POL-01 and the facility security plan maintained by the Director of Facilities.
Badge access authorizations are approved by department leaders and reviewed quarterly for the data center, pharmacy, and nursery.
Badge access protects the data center, pharmacy, nursery (with infant protection), ED entrance, and 32 of 41 network closets; 9 closets use keys with no key log.
Video and badge logs cover the data center and pharmacy; badge alarms go to security officers. Network closet access is not monitored.
evidence: Video coverage map; badge alarm log

implementation_statement: Visitors to the data center sign a log and are escorted.
The data center is on the generator-backed critical power branch with an uninterruptible power supply sized for 30 minutes; generator testing follows NFPA 110 as 482.15(e) requires.
Redundant cooling with temperature and humidity monitoring alerts facilities engineers 24x7.
Planning requirements are in POL-01; the SSP is maintained under this plan (P02).
This SSP documents HECS, its boundary, and its controls; it is reviewed each year and after major changes.
All workforce members sign the acceptable use policy (POL-05) at hire and each year. Affiliated practice users sign it once at account creation; agency nurses are not tracked.

implementation_statement: The information security program plan is POL-01 with the standards index and this SSP (tailoring: added; not in the Moderate baseline).

implementation_statement: The IT Director is designated in writing as HIPAA Security Officer; the vCISO leads program strategy (tailoring: added).

baseline: Added by tailoring (not in Moderate baseline)
implementation_statement: A risk management strategy with appetite statements and acceptance authority was approved in 2026-09 (P01). Before then, risk acceptance was informal (tailoring: added).
Personnel security requirements are in POL-02 and HR policies.

Employees are background-checked before hire. Contracted clinicians are credentialed by the Medical Staff Office; agency nurses are screened by their agencies under contract, but the hospital does not verify it.

Employee terminations disable access the same day through the HR feed. Badges, local device accounts, and shared vendor passwords are not covered. Non-employee terminations depend on agencies and practices to notify the hospital.
Transfers trigger a role change in the identity provider, but EHR roles from the prior department are not removed automatically.
Contracts with the physician groups, staffing agencies, and affiliated practices require confidentiality and departure notice. Notice terms are not enforced and 19 departed users kept access (gap 8).
regulatory_driver: C-HPH-R08 (CPG Essential: Revoke Credentials for Departing Workforce Members)

implementation_statement: The HIPAA sanctions policy is applied by the Privacy Officer and HR; 11 sanctions were documented in 2025-2026.
Risk assessment requirements are in POL-01; the P01 method (NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1) is documented.
HECS is categorized Moderate (section 6). Medical devices and OT are not yet categorized individually.
The 2026 enterprise risk analysis (P01) covers the hospital, HECS, OT, communications, vendors, and AI. It cannot be fully accurate while the device inventory is 70% complete.
Supply chain risks are assessed at vendor onboarding only; Tier 1 vendors are not reassessed (gap 6).

Authenticated vulnerability scans of IT assets run quarterly; the cloud posture service scans continuously. Medical devices and OT are not scanned, even passively (gap 1). Critical findings average 41 days to fix against a 30-day target.
The scanner updates its vulnerability checks before each scan; the team reviews the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog weekly.
evidence: Scanner update logs; weekly review notes

implementation_statement: Risk responses are recorded in the P01 register with owners and dates and tracked in the P07 POA&M.
Critical components are identified through the BIA (P05) and the applications and data criticality analysis.

New contracts include security and BAA terms. Medical device purchases do not require an MDS2 form, a software bill of materials, or a support-period commitment, which FD&C Act sec. 524B now makes available from manufacturers of cyber devices.

control_name: Use of Live or Operational Data
baseline: Added by tailoring (not in Moderate baseline)
implementation_statement: Production PHI must not be used in test environments (POL-04 4.5). The interface engine test environment still holds copies of production messages with PHI and is reachable by 9 interface analysts and 2 vendor engineers (gap 11); synthetic data due 2026-12-31 (tailoring: added).
External services with PHI are covered by BAAs for 168 of about 210 vendors (gap 6). Tier 1 vendors provide SOC 2 reports at onboarding only; the PACS vendor has none.
regulatory_driver: C-HPH-R01 (164.308(b)(1); 164.308(b)(3); 164.314(a); 164.314(a)(2)(i); 164.314(a)(2)(iii); 164.314(a)(3)(i)); C-HPH-R08 (CPG Essential: Vendor/Supplier Cybersecurity Requirements)

implementation_statement: 210 medical devices run unsupported operating systems, including the catheterization lab hemodynamic system, the fetal surveillance server, and 2 laboratory analyzer workstations. Compensating controls (VLAN, allowlisting) exist only for imaging modalities.
System and communications protection requirements are in POL-04; the encryption standard (STD-08) dates from 2023.
Carrier and cloud provider denial-of-service protection covers internet links and public endpoints (the portal is vendor-hosted).
Perimeter firewalls and the cloud hub firewall control traffic with logging. Internal segmentation is partial: pumps and imaging are isolated; other devices and building OT are not (gaps 1 and 13).
Internet access passes through 2 managed access points at the main campus and the cloud hub; the outpatient center routes through the campus.

control_name: Deny by Default - Allow by Exception
implementation_statement: Deny-by-default rules apply at the perimeter, the cloud hub, and the pump and imaging VLANs. The clinical VLAN and OT network allow any-to-any traffic internally.
EHR, portal, interface, and remote access traffic uses TLS 1.2 or higher or IPsec. Legacy HL7 feeds between the LIS and analyzers on campus are unencrypted but stay on the data center network.
Cloud workloads use hospital-managed keys in the cloud key management service; backup keys are separate.
FIPS-validated cryptographic modules are used by the cloud provider, EHR vendor, VPN, and endpoint encryption.

provider_if_inherited: Cloud provider (SOC 2 Type 2); EHR vendor (SOC 2 Type 2)
implementation_statement: Laptops, workstations, servers, cloud storage, and backups are encrypted. Many medical devices (ultrasound units, monitors, analyzers) store ePHI locally without encryption.
Workstations and servers are patched monthly. Vendor-managed servers and medical devices are patched only when manufacturers release validated updates; 210 devices cannot be patched.
EDR runs on all managed workstations and servers and is monitored 24x7; medical devices that cannot run EDR rely on network controls.
The MSSP monitors EDR and SIEM alerts 24x7. There is no network monitoring for medical devices or OT and no egress alerting for the data warehouse and file services.
regulatory_driver: C-HPH-R01 (164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D)); C-HPH-R08 (CPG Enhanced: Detect and Respond to Relevant Threats and Tactics)

implementation_statement: Perimeter and cloud firewall logs are monitored for known bad destinations; volume-based egress alerting is not configured.
The team receives CISA, HHS HC3, and Health-ISAC alerts and FDA device safety communications and reviews them weekly.
The EHR vendor maintains record integrity controls. The hospital does not monitor integrity of the infusion pump drug library server, dispensing cabinet server, or interface engine mappings.
evidence: EHR vendor SOC 2; pump server review

implementation_statement: The email security gateway filters spam and malware. DMARC is at p=none and external sender tagging is off (gap 12).
The interface engine validates HL7 message structure; patient-matching errors from the reference laboratory interface (12 in 2026) are caught by HIM reconciliation, not by validation rules.

Policies, risk analyses, assessments, and incident records are kept 6 years; medical records follow the HIM retention schedule (at least 5 years under 42 CFR 482.24(b)(1), longer where Florida law requires).
Supply chain risk is addressed in POL-01 4.9-4.10; the vendor risk management standard (STD-03) is in draft.
Tier 1 vendors are not reassessed after onboarding. The P09 vendor review program starts annual reviews of the 15 Tier 1 vendors.
